opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few reasons that point is particularly attractive as a place to pause, or at least to slow down a lot.

The first is that it's roughly the point where things could start going very fast. Once you have AIs that can fully automate the work of an AI company (the research, the engineering, running experiments), you plausibly get a big acceleration in AI progress. Instead of being bottlenecked on a few thousand human researchers, you have huge numbers of AI researchers working in parallel, running faster than humans. So you might go from "roughly human-level at AI R&D" to "very superhuman" in a fairly short period, maybe a year or less. If you're going to pause, pausing before that intelligence explosion kicks off seems much better than trying to pause in the middle of it, when things are moving extremely quickly and the systems are much harder to oversee.

The second reason is that around that level of capability, the AIs are actually really useful for safety work. If you pause much earlier, you don't have AIs that can meaningfully help you with alignment research, interpretability, building better control measures, and so on. You're just waiting, and humans are doing all the work at human speed. But at the point where AIs can automate an AI company, you could redirect a huge amount of that labor toward safety. You get to use the systems to help figure out how to make the next systems safe. So you capture a lot of the benefit while not yet taking on the risks of systems that are vastly superhuman.

Third, I think these systems are plausibly still controllable in a way that much more capable systems might not be. With systems around human level, even if they're misaligned, I think there's a reasonable chance that techniques like monitoring, control protocols, and careful security can stop them from causing catastrophic outcomes, and that we can catch them if they're trying to do something bad. That gets much harder once you're dealing with things that are wildly smarter than us. So it's a sweet spot: capable enough to be extremely useful, not so capable that we've lost the ability to keep them in check.

And finally, there's a legibility point. Before you reach that level, it's quite hard to convince people that the risks are real and imminent, because the systems still look like tools with obvious limitations. Once AIs can do essentially everything an AI company does, I think it becomes much more salient to governments and the public that we're at a really pivotal moment. So the political will for a coordinated pause might actually exist then, in a way that it doesn't today.

To be clear, I'm not saying pausing is easy, or that it's likely to happen. There are huge coordination problems, especially internationally. But if you ask me where the best place to spend a limited amount of "pause budget" is, say a year or a few years of slowdown, I think it's much better spent right around that point than now, and much better than after you've already blown past it.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss Ryan Greenblatt’s timeline estimates or say they assume no very active intervention.

r002.rationale: It says AI labor could be redirected toward safety work, but does not identify giving humans additional time to study AI systems as a benefit of an extended pause.

r003.rationale: It discusses safety and controlling catastrophic outcomes, but does not state that extracting labor from AI systems could reduce the ongoing risk of AI takeover.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic picture is that I think there are a few things that make that specific point a lot more attractive than pausing either much earlier or much later.

The first thing is just that by the time you have AIs that can fully automate an AI company, you already have systems that are enormously useful. You can get a lot of the benefits of AI without necessarily pushing to wildly superhuman systems. These AIs could do huge amounts of alignment research, interpretability research, security work, and so on. So a pause at that point isn't really a pause in the sense of "nothing is happening" — it's more like you're redirecting an enormous amount of cognitive labour toward making the situation safer rather than toward making the systems more capable. That's very different from pausing today, where the systems can't really do much of that work for you.

The second thing is about verifiability and coordination. If the key actors agree to pause at roughly that capability level, it's a reasonably legible threshold. You can point to a system and say, "Okay, this can basically do everything an AI researcher does." It's a lot harder to coordinate around some vague notion of "the systems are getting dangerous," because people will just disagree about whether that's true. A relatively concrete milestone makes the deal easier to strike and easier to monitor.

The third thing, which I think is actually the most important, is the shape of the risk. My view is that a large fraction of the risk comes from the transition where you go from roughly human-level systems to systems that are qualitatively much smarter than us — and where that transition happens really fast because the AIs themselves are doing the research. If you let that intelligence explosion run with basically no human oversight, you end up with systems that are very hard to understand, very hard to control, and you've compressed years of progress into months. If you instead deliberately slow down right at the start of that, you can take the time to actually check whether these systems are aligned, develop better techniques, and make the next steps more gradual. You've got a lot of leverage at that point and you haven't yet lost the ability to intervene.

And I'd add — I'm not saying I'm confident this would go well. It still requires a lot of political will, it requires the leading actors to actually be willing to do this, and there are real concerns about what happens if some actor doesn't comply. But if you asked me, "At what point does pausing look like it buys you the most safety for the least cost?" I think it's right around there. Earlier, you lose a lot of the benefits and you don't have the AI labour to help you; later, you might already have lost control of the situation.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a point where the case for pausing becomes much more concrete. You can say, “These systems can now do essentially all the work involved in building the next generation of AI.” So there’s a pretty direct argument that further progress could be very fast, and that we might not have much time to respond once we go beyond that point.

At the same time, you’d have extremely useful systems for doing safety research. If you could pause further capability development while using those systems to work on alignment and evaluate the risks, you could potentially make a lot of progress without needing to build something more capable first.

That’s conditional on being able to use those systems safely, and on the pause actually being enforced. Neither is guaranteed. But it seems like a comparatively promising place to stop: the danger is more legible, and you have much better tools for addressing it.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, at that point you might have a much better alternative to continuing to build more powerful AI: you could use the systems you already have to do a huge amount of AI safety research. If they can automate an AI company, they can presumably automate a lot of the work involved in understanding and aligning the next generation of systems.

So the proposal would be to pause increases in capability while using those existing systems to figure out how to proceed safely. That seems more promising than pausing much earlier, when you’re still relying on humans to solve all these problems.

The big caveat is that you need those systems to be sufficiently trustworthy, or sufficiently well controlled, that the research they produce actually helps. And it’s not obvious that there’s a comfortable gap between “can automate an AI company” and “poses an unacceptable risk.” But if that gap exists, it seems like a particularly valuable place to stop and do the safety work.
